plain_title: First transistors and solar cells in orbit
plain_text: Months after Sputnik's radio beep, tiny silicon and germanium transistors count cosmic rays above Earth's atmosphere and discover the Van Allen radiation belts.
power_source: Mercury batteries (Explorer 1) & first silicon solar cells (Vanguard 1)
active_2026: Historical (Vanguard 1 hull still in orbit, silent since 1964)
source: Van Allen et al. (1958) Jet Propulsion 28:588; Richter et al. (1959) IRE Trans. Mil. Electron. MIL-3:96
note: Sputnik 1 (Oct 1957) used vacuum-tube radio oscillators; Explorer 1 (Jan 1958) and Vanguard 1 (Mar 1958) brought solid-state electronics and solar power to space.

mission_or_system: Mariner 4 Central Computer & Endless-Loop Tape Recorder
plain_title: First digital pictures from another planet
plain_text: Mariner 4 records 21 digital close-ups of Mars onto magnetic tape and trickles the 1s and 0s home at 8 bits a second—taking over eight hours per photo.
processor_hardware: Fixed-sequence Central Computer & Sequencer (38.4 kHz crystal)
power_source: Four solar panels (170 W at Mars)
source: Leighton et al. (1965) Science 149:627; Tomayko (1988) Computers in Spaceflight: The NASA Experience (NASA SP-4212)
note: Engineers hand-colored a paper printout of the numeric pixel brightness values while waiting for film processing.

plain_title: First reprogrammable computer flown by astronauts
plain_text: Astronauts in Earth orbit use a magnetic-core computer to calculate orbital rendezvous and steer controlled reentries—reloading new programs from magnetic tape mid-flight.
processor_hardware: Discrete silicon transistor CPU + 39-bit ferrite magnetic core
source: Tomayko (1988) NASA SP-4212 Ch. 1; IBM Federal Systems Division (1966) Gemini Guidance Computer Report
note: 140-microsecond addition cycle; auxiliary magnetic tape multiplied program capacity sevenfold starting on Gemini 8.

mission_or_system: Apollo Block II Guidance Computer (Command & Lunar Modules)
plain_title: 72 kilobytes land humans on the Moon
plain_text: Built from 5,600 early silicon microchips and hand-woven copper core-rope memory, Apollo's computer drops unimportant tasks mid-descent to land Eagle safely on the Moon.
processor_hardware: ~5,600 Fairchild RTL NOR gate ICs (2.048 MHz clock)
power_source: Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells & lunar-module silver-zinc batteries
active_2026: Historical (descent stages remain on the Moon)
source: Hall (1996) Journey to the Moon: The History of the Apollo Guidance Computer (AIAA); Hamilton & Hackler (2008) IEEE Comput. 41(11):76
note: 4 KB erasable ferrite-core RAM + 72 KB read-only core rope; priority-interrupt executive resolved famous 1201/1202 alarms during Apollo 11 touchdown.

plain_title: First electronics past the asteroid belt and Jupiter
plain_text: Powered by plutonium heat where sunlight dims, Pioneer 10 survives Jupiter's fierce radiation belts and carries a gold-anodized plaque on a path out of the Solar System.
processor_hardware: Hardwired TTL digital command decoder & 5-command buffer
power_source: Four SNAP-19 plutonium-238 RTGs (155 W at launch)
active_2026: Silent in outer heliosphere / interstellar coast (last signal Jan 2003 at 80 AU)
source: Fimmel, Swindell & Burgess (1980) Pioneer Odyssey (NASA SP-349); Sagan, Sagan & Drake (1972) Science 175:881
note: Distance shown at final radio contact in 2003 (12.2 billion km); by 2026 Pioneer 10 coasts silently near ~139 AU.

plain_title: First computer to land itself on another planet
plain_text: With radio signals taking nearly twenty minutes to reach Mars, Viking's plated-wire computer fires its own retrorockets and runs automated soil chemistry labs with no human hand on the stick.
processor_hardware: Dual Honeywell 24-bit GCSC with 2-mil plated-wire memory
power_source: Two SNAP-19 plutonium-238 RTGs (70 W continuous on Mars)
active_2026: Dormant on Chryse & Utopia Planitia, Mars (active 1976–1982)
source: Tomayko (1988) NASA SP-4212 Ch. 6; Soffen (1977) J. Geophys. Res. 82:3959
note: Magnetic plated-wire memory kept its bits without power and shrugged off cosmic rays; Viking 1 operated for over six Earth years.

mission_or_system: Voyager 1 & Voyager 2 Six-Computer Suite + Golden Records
plain_title: Voyager 1 & 2 launch with 69 KB of memory and a billion-year record
plain_text: Two twin probes depart Earth carrying six redundant 1970s computers totaling 69 kilobytes of memory, an 8-track digital tape deck, and gold-plated copper records built to outlast continents.
processor_hardware: 6 computers (dual 18-bit CCS + dual 16-bit CMOS FDS + dual 18-bit AACS)
power_source: Three MHW plutonium-238 RTGs (470 W at 1977 launch)
active_2026: Yes — both probes still active in interstellar space in 2026
source: Kohlhase & Penzo (1977) Space Sci. Rev. 21:77; Tomayko (1988) NASA SP-4212; Sagan et al. (1978) Murmurs of Earth
note: Downlink reached 115.2 kbps at Jupiter (1979) and 21.6 kbps at Neptune (1989, ~4.5B km); each Golden Record adds ~1.5 gigabits of analog images, speech and music rated for ~1 billion years.

plain_title: First microprocessors brave Jupiter's radiation belts
plain_text: Six sapphire-insulated 8-bit microprocessors steer Galileo through radiation strong enough to fry an ordinary laptop in seconds, compressing photos onboard when its main antenna jams.
processor_hardware: Six RCA CDP1802 COSMAC 8-bit CMOS-on-sapphire microprocessors (1.6 MHz)
power_source: Two GPHS plutonium-238 RTGs (570 W at launch)
active_2026: Historical (intentionally plunged into Jupiter in 2003 to protect Europa)
source: Tomayko (1988) NASA SP-4212 Ch. 6; Meltzer (2007) Mission to Jupiter (NASA SP-2007-4231)
note: When Galileo's high-gain dish failed to unfurl, JPL uploaded modern ICT image-compression software to its 1802 chips to rescue the mission over a 160 bps low-gain antenna.

plain_title: An orbital eye upgraded in space by astronauts
plain_text: Orbiting above Earth's blurry air, Hubble locks onto galaxies to billionths of a degree and receives a 20-times faster silicon brain and solid-state memory from visiting shuttle crews.
processor_hardware: Rockwell DF-224 (1990), upgraded in 1999 to radiation-hardened Intel 80486 (25 MHz)
power_source: Twin gallium-arsenide solar wings + nickel-hydrogen batteries
active_2026: Yes — still observing in low Earth orbit after 36 years
source: Zimmerman (2008) The Universe in a Mirror; NASA Goddard Hubble Servicing Mission 3A Technical Report (1999)
note: Solid-state recorders (12 gigabytes = 9.6×10^10 bits) replaced mechanical reel-to-reel tape decks in orbit.

plain_title: First autonomous wheeled rover explores Mars
plain_text: Shoebox-sized Sojourner uses laser stripes and an 8-bit chip to dodge boulders on its own while its lander inaugurates the 32-bit RAD6000 radiation-hardened computer.
processor_hardware: IBM/BAE RAD6000 32-bit RISC (20 MHz lander) + Intel 80C85 (2 MHz rover)
power_source: Gallium-arsenide solar arrays (35 W lander, 16 W rover)
source: Bajracharya, Maimone & Helmick (2008) Computer 41(12):44; Shirley (1998) Managing Martians
note: A famous priority-inversion bug on Mars was diagnosed on Earth and patched remotely in VxWorks, proving complex real-time operating systems could be maintained across interplanetary space.

mission_or_system: Cassini Saturn Orbiter & Huygens Titan Lander
plain_title: Solid-state memory orbits Saturn and lands on Titan
plain_text: With no moving tape parts to wear out, Cassini orbits Saturn for thirteen years and drops the Huygens probe onto hydrocarbon-shrouded Titan 1.4 billion km from Earth.
processor_hardware: Dual MIL-STD-1750A GVSC 16-bit radiation-hardened CPUs + Huygens dual CDMS
power_source: Three GPHS plutonium-238 RTGs (885 W at launch)
active_2026: Historical (Cassini plunged into Saturn in 2017; Huygens rests on Titan)
source: Matson, Spilker & Lebreton (2002) Space Sci. Rev. 104:1; Lebreton et al. (2005) Nature 438:758
note: Huygens remains humanity's most distant planetary landing (~1.4 billion km, January 2005).

mission_or_system: New Horizons Pluto & Kuiper Belt Probe (Mongoose-V)
plain_title: Flash-memory probe maps Pluto and cruises the Kuiper Belt
plain_text: Four radiation-hardened processors and 16 gigabytes of flash memory capture Pluto and icy Arrokoth up close, then spend sixteen months beaming the archive home across six billion km.
processor_hardware: Four Synova Mongoose-V 32-bit radiation-hardened MIPS R3000 CPUs (12 MHz)
power_source: Single GPHS plutonium-238 RTG (~240 W at launch, ~185 W in Kuiper Belt)
active_2026: Yes — active in the Kuiper Belt at ~64.2 AU (9.61 billion km) in 2026
source: Fountain et al. (2008) Space Sci. Rev. 140:23; Stern et al. (2015) Science 350:aad1815; Stern et al. (2019) Science 364:aaw9771
note: Distance shown is late-2026 Kuiper Belt position (~64.2 AU); New Horizons is the fifth spacecraft escaping the Sun and one of three still active.

mission_or_system: Curiosity Rover (RAD750 + AEGIS Autonomous Target Selection)
plain_title: A Mars rover chooses its own rocks to zap with a laser
plain_text: Instead of sitting idle after each drive waiting half an hour for Earth's instructions, Curiosity runs onboard computer vision to spot interesting outcrops and fire its laser spectrometer itself.
processor_hardware: Dual BAE RAD750 32-bit radiation-hardened PowerPC CPUs (200 MHz)
power_source: Plutonium-238 Multi-Mission RTG + lithium-ion buffer batteries
active_2026: Yes — climbing Mount Sharp in Gale Crater in 2026
source: Grotzinger et al. (2012) Space Sci. Rev. 170:5; Francis et al. (2017) Sci. Robot. 2:eaan4582
note: Up to 2 Mbps UHF relay via Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter; AEGIS autonomous targeting boosted geochemical hit rate from ~24% (blind) to >93%.

mission_or_system: Perseverance Rover (RAD750 + Vision FPGA) & Ingenuity Helicopter (Snapdragon 801)
plain_title: A smartphone chip flies 72 autonomous sorties in Mars's thin air
plain_text: Ingenuity pairs a commercial Linux smartphone processor with a radiation-tolerant watchdog to track ground features 30 times a second—bringing 100 times more single-chip compute to Mars than every earlier mission combined.
processor_hardware: Perseverance RAD750 & Virtex-5 Vision FPGA + Ingenuity Snapdragon 801 (2.26 GHz ARM Linux)
power_source: Perseverance MMRTG (110 W) + Ingenuity solar-charged Li-ion pack (~20 W flight)
active_2026: Perseverance active in Jezero Crater; Ingenuity retired Jan 2024 after 72 flights
source: Balaram et al. (2021) Space Sci. Rev. 217:56; Verma et al. (2023) Sci. Robot. 8:eadf8058
note: Continuous active Mars rover compute is ~1.5×10^9 executed ops/s (RAD750 + Vision Compute FPGA, ~5× faster than Curiosity); during its 72 brief 90-second sorties (2021–2024), Ingenuity's Snapdragon 801 burst up to ~2×10^10 ops/s.

mission_or_system: James Webb Space Telescope (Sun–Earth L2, 1.5 Million km)
plain_title: An infrared observatory computes 1.5 million km beyond Earth
plain_text: Parked four times farther than the Moon behind a tennis-court sunshield at 40 kelvin, Webb collects and compresses nearly half a terabit of deep-universe light every day.
processor_hardware: BAE RAD750 (118 MHz) + custom cryogenic SIDECAR ASIC focal-plane digitizers
power_source: 6-meter solar array on sunward bus (2 kW continuous)
active_2026: Yes — operating at Sun–Earth Lagrange Point L2
source: Gardner et al. (2023) Publ. Astron. Soc. Pac. 135:068001; Loose et al. (2007) Proc. SPIE 6690
note: Cryogenic SIDECAR ASICs digitize infrared pixels right at 37 K next to the mirrors before handing frames to the 58.9 GB solid-state recorder.

mission_or_system: DART SMART Nav Autonomous Asteroid Redirector & Psyche Deep-Space Laser
plain_title: A spacecraft steers itself into an asteroid and lasers beam video from deep space
plain_text: Eleven million km from Earth, DART spots moonlet Dimorphos and guides itself to impact at 6 km/s with zero human steering, while NASA's Psyche laser beams 267 megabits a second across interplanetary space.
processor_hardware: BAE RAD750 running SMART Nav optical guidance + flight photon-counting laser transceiver
power_source: Roll-Out Solar Arrays (ROSA) & Hall-effect solar electric propulsion
active_2026: DART impacted Sept 2022 (Hera inspecting crater 2026); Psyche active en route to asteroid belt
source: Daly et al. (2023) Nature 616:443; Biswas et al. (2024) JPL Deep Space Optical Communications Report
note: Psyche's Deep Space Optical Communications (DSOC) achieved 267 Mbps at 31M km and 25 Mbps at 226M km—1.6 million times Voyager 1's bit rate.

mission_or_system: Voyager 1 Crosses One Light-Day from Earth (Nov 2026, ~173 AU)
plain_title: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth—and is still computing
plain_text: Forty-nine years after launch, humanity's farthest computer crosses 25.9 billion km (24 hours of light travel one way), whispering plasma and magnetic data home at 160 bits a second on a 23-watt radio.
processor_hardware: Surviving 1970s CCS/FDS/AACS processors (remotely patched across 24B km in 2024)
power_source: Decaying plutonium-238 RTGs (~215 W remaining of original 470 W)
active_2026: Yes — operating at 1.00 light-day (~173.1 AU); twin Voyager 2 active at ~144.3 AU
source: Stone et al. (2013) Science 341:150; Burlaga et al. (2021) Nat. Astron. 5:478; NASA JPL Voyager Mission Status (Nov 2026)
note: In 2024 JPL engineers diagnosed a dead FDS memory chip and rewrote Voyager 1's flight code into tiny surviving memory blocks across a 45-hour round-trip radio delay. Storage includes Golden Record (~1.5 Gb analog-equivalent, ~10^9-year interstellar persistence).

mission_or_system: Total Active Off-Earth Computing Fleet (~17,500 Satellites & ~40 Deep-Space Probes)
plain_title: 17,500 spacecraft wrap Earth in lasers—yet hold 0.00001% of our compute
plain_text: Laser-linked satellite shells, ISS edge servers, L2 telescopes, nine Mars robots and two interstellar Voyagers extend sensing 25.9 billion km out, yet together run less compute than two datacenter AI racks on Earth.
power_source: ~42 MW orbital solar arrays + ~1.5 kW deep-space Pu-238 RTGs
source: McDowell (2026) Jonathan's Space Report / Planet4589; ESA Space Environment Report (2025); NASA Deep Space Network Now (2026)
note: 1.9×10^15 executed ops/s off Earth ÷ 1.89×10^22 executed ops/s on Earth = 1.0×10^-7 (0.00001%). Deep space beyond the Moon accounts for only ~3×10^10 ops/s—less than one modern smartphone.
